claim: Two rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in the study with weights of 5-7 kg and ages of 5 and 7 years.
source: Two adult male Rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in the study (weight: 5–7 kg, age: 5, 7 years).
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the subjects

claim: Experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics in Research Committee of the Institute of Neurobiology and were in agreement with the principles outlined in the Guide for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Institutes of Health).
source: Experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics in Research Committee of the Institute of Neurobiology and were in agreement with the principles outlined in the Guide for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Institutes of Health).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval and compliance

claim: Each monkey was surgically implanted with titanium head bolts and a titanium recording chamber over the left supplementary motor area (SMA).
source: Each monkey was surgically implanted with titanium head bolts and a titanium recording chamber over the left supplementary motor area (SMA).
evidence: Direct statement of surgical procedures performed

claim: Placement of the chambers over the SMA was guided by structural MRI for both monkeys.
source: Placement of the chambers over the SMA was guided by structural MRI for both monkeys (Figure 1E).
evidence: Statement about surgical guidance method with reference to figure showing recording location

claim: Monkeys performed a visual metronome task while maintaining eye and hand fixation over a touch screen.
source: Monkeys were trained in a visual metronome task described in detail in a previous report (García-Garibay et al., 2016). Briefly, while maintain eye and hand fixation over a touch screen (ELO Touch Solutions, model 1939L; ASL Eye-Track 6), subjects observed a visual stimulus (gray circle, 10° diameter, 25° eccentricity) that periodically changed position from one side of the screen to the other, at regular intervals (entrainment epoch; 500, 750, or 1000 ms interval; pseudo-randomly selected on each trial; Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of behavioral task with citation to previous work and reference to figure

claim: The interval duration in the visual metronome task was pseudo-randomly chosen to be 500, 750, or 1000 ms on each trial.
source: On each trial, the interval duration was pseudo-randomly chosen to be 500, 750, or 1000 ms.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design parameters

claim: After three entrainment intervals, the visual stimulus disappeared and subjects had to maintain the rhythm internally.
source: After the third entrainment interval, the visual stimulus disappeared, and subjects had to maintain the rhythm internally by keeping track of the virtual position (left or right) of the stimulus as a function of elapsed time.
evidence: Description of task structure

claim: The visual metronome task was not an interception task because the left-right switching stopped at the time of the go-cue.
source: It is important to note that this was not an interception task, that is once the go-cue was presented the non-visible stimulus no longer changed position.
evidence: Explicit clarification of task design

claim: Monkeys correctly estimated the location of the stimulus in more than 80% of trials (94 ± 0.2% monkey 1; 86 ± 0.3% monkey 2).
source: The behavioral results show that monkeys satisfactorily performed the task and were able to correctly estimate the location of the stimulus in more than 80% of trials (94 ± 0.2% monkey 1; 86 ± 0.3% monkey 2; mean ± s.e. over sessions, n = 131 sessions).
evidence: Quantitative behavioral performance data

claim: The proportion of correct responses declined as a function of the number of maintenance intervals.
source: Importantly, performance as a function of time displays the hallmark of a timing task: the proportion of correct responses declines as a function of the number of maintenance intervals (or equivalently, elapsed time).
evidence: Description of behavioral pattern observed in the data

claim: The proportion of correct responses started close to 100% and declined to approximately 75% for the last maintenance intervals.
source: The proportion of correct responses started close to 100% and declined to approximately 75% for the last maintenance intervals (last two data points for each curve).
evidence: Quantitative description of behavioral performance pattern

claim: The decline in performance is consistent with the internal rhythm gradually drifting away from the true tempo of the stimulus.
source: This behavior is consistent with the internal rhythm gradually drifting away from the true tempo of the stimulus (Gibbon et al., 1997; Grondin, 2001).
evidence: Interpretation of behavioral data with citations to supporting literature

claim: The pattern of performance decline is well captured by a model in which the subject's time estimates arise from increasingly noisy distributions, described by Weber's Law of time.
source: As we described in previous work (García-Garibay et al., 2016), this pattern is well captured by a model in which the subject's time estimates arise from increasingly noisy (wider) distributions, described by Weber's Law of time (also called the scalar property of timing) (Laje et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of model fit to behavioral data with citations

claim: The increase in timing variability causes subjects to eventually fall out of synchrony with the true stimulus position.
source: The increase in timing variability causes the subjects to eventually fall out of synchrony with the true stimulus position (getting ahead, or behind the true tempo), thus explaining the decrease in correct responses as a function of elapsed time (Figure 1B, the colored curves are fits of this model to the data; pooled data across monkeys; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Explanation of behavioral pattern with reference to model and figures

claim: Behavioral performance for the 4th maintenance interval of the 750 and 1000 ms tempos is higher than would be expected from the model.
source: Behavioral performance for the 4th maintenance interval of the 750 and 1000 ms tempos is higher than would be expected, that is it is higher than the performance on the previous 3rd interval.
evidence: Observation of deviation from expected pattern

claim: Monkeys likely exploited the information that the experiment only included up to four maintenance intervals and halted maintenance at the 4th interval to avoid errors.
source: This is likely due to the fact that our experiment only included up to four maintenance intervals. We speculate that monkeys exploited this information and halted the maintenance at the 4th interval, so that they could avoid errors due to moving onto the 5th interval.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed behavioral pattern

claim: Reaction times to the go-cue increase significantly in proportion to elapsed time within a narrow window ranging between 350 ms to 400 ms.
source: Reaction times to the go-cue increases significantly in proportion to elapsed time within a narrow window ranging between 350 ms after the first maintenance interval of the fastest tempo (500 ms intervals), to 400 ms after the last interval of the slowest tempo (1000 ms intervals) (Figure 1C; R2 = 0.72, slope = 11 ms/s, p<0.001; monkey 1 = 10.2 ms/s±0.8; monkey 2 = 11.3 ms/s ± 0.5).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of reaction time data with statistical measures

claim: The increase in reaction times could be a result of the increasing difficulty in estimating the true stimulus position.
source: This increase in reaction times could be a result of the increasing difficulty in estimating the true stimulus position.
evidence: Interpretation of reaction time data

claim: Larger gamma band amplitudes are correlated with increased reaction times.
source: We also demonstrate that larger gamma band amplitudes are correlated with increased reaction times.
evidence: Statement about correlation analysis with reference to supplementary figure

claim: Gamma band activity decreases and is replaced by low-frequency oscillations at movement onset.
source: In Figure 1—figure supplement 2, we provide the LFP spectrogram aligned to movement onset, demonstrating that gamma band activity decreases, and it is replaced by low-frequency oscillations at movement onset.
evidence: Description of neural activity pattern with reference to figure

claim: Monkeys were able to entrain to a rhythm and maintain it in the absence of sensory stimuli and overt motor commands.
source: Overall, behavioral results show that monkeys were able to entrain to a rhythm, and maintain it in the absence of sensory stimuli, and importantly, in the absence of overt motor commands.
evidence: Summary statement of behavioral findings

claim: Neural activity was recorded in 131 experimental sessions (84 and 47 for monkeys 1 and 2, respectively).
source: While the monkeys performed the visual metronome task, we recorded neural activity in 131 experimental sessions (84 and 47 for monkeys 1 and 2, respectively; Figure 1E), and analyzed the local field potentials (LFPs) within 5–80 Hz band.
evidence: Statement of data collection parameters

claim: LFP power in the 30-40 Hz gamma band was up to two-fold larger than baseline activity recorded 500 ms before trial initiation.
source: In this band, LFP power was up to two-fold larger than the baseline activity recorded 500 ms before trial initiation (p<0.001; permutation test of the time-frequency bins, 1000 permutations).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test

claim: LFP amplitude in the gamma band had a rhythmic structure that increased markedly with the presentation of the last visible stimulus and near the time when the non-visible stimulus would be switching positions.
source: The LFP amplitude in the gamma band had a rhythmic structure. It increased markedly with the presentation of the last visible stimulus (3rd entrainment interval, Figure 1D), as well as near the time when the non-visible stimulus would be switching its position from one side of the screen to the other during maintenance intervals (Figure 1D; broken red lines).
evidence: Description of observed neural pattern with reference to figure

claim: The average gamma amplitude at the time of switches was significantly higher than halfway between them.
source: To test this observation quantitatively, we verified that the average gamma amplitude at the time of switches was significantly higher than halfway between them (t-test, p<0.01 for the three tempos; window sizes 1/4th of interval length; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical test of observed pattern

claim: Gamma oscillations increased in amplitude as a function of total elapsed time.
source: In addition to the rhythmic modulation, gamma oscillations increased in amplitude as a function of total elapsed time (Figures 1D and 3C; note that the last maintenance interval displays the largest amplitude).
evidence: Description of observed pattern with reference to figures

claim: LFP recordings from single trials revealed short-duration bursts during which oscillations transiently increase in amplitude.
source: The LFP recordings from single trials (band-passed at 30–40 Hz) revealed short-duration bursts during which the oscillations transiently increase in amplitude (Figure 2B), consistent with recent findings in the putamen (Bartolo et al., 2014) and the prefrontal cortex (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of single-trial analysis with citations to similar findings

claim: During the maintenance epoch, gamma bursts tended to coincide with the times at which the stimulus would have changed position.
source: Importantly, we observed that during the maintenance epoch, these bursts tended to coincide with the times at which the stimulus would have changed position, as is shown by the peaks in the spectrogram of the example single trials (Figure 2A).
evidence: Description of temporal relationship between neural activity and task structure

claim: Gamma bursts during maintenance tend to appear around the times at which the stimulus should be switching from one side of the screen to the other.
source: It is readily apparent that gamma bursts during maintenance tend to appear around the times at which the stimulus should be switching from one side of the screen to the other.
evidence: Description of pattern visible in single-trial data visualization

claim: Mean gamma amplitude at times of switch (0.5 and 1 s) was significantly higher than amplitudes at the middle of the interval (0.75 and 1.25 s).
source: This pattern is captured by the mean gamma amplitude, across trials, as a function of elapsed time (Figure 2D; p<0.01, t-test that compared amplitudes at the times of switch [0.5 and 1 s] versus amplitudes at the middle of the interval [0.75 and 1.25 s]; 125 ms windows).
evidence: Statistical test of mean activity pattern

claim: The salient temporal features of gamma LFP were consistent across the three interval durations (500, 750, and 1000 ms).
source: These salient temporal features of the gamma LFP were consistent across the three interval durations (Figure 3A; 500, 750, and 1000 ms intervals).
evidence: Statement of consistency across conditions with figure reference

claim: There are no motor actions during the maintenance intervals and no periodic stimuli shown on the screen.
source: It is important to emphasize that there are no motor actions during the maintenance intervals, and no periodic stimuli is shown on the screen.
evidence: Explicit statement of task design constraints

claim: The only difference between the three groups of trials (500, 750, 1000 ms) is the tempo of the internal rhythm that subjects are maintaining.
source: The only difference between the three groups of trials (500, 750, 1000 ms) is the tempo of the internal rhythm that subjects are maintaining.
evidence: Statement about experimental design and interpretation

claim: The rapid succession of gamma bursts in the 500 ms intervals and the more temporally distant bursts in the 1000 ms intervals are a reflection of the subject's internal maintenance of a visuo-spatial rhythm for fast and slow tempos.
source: In other words, the rapid succession of the gamma bursts in the 500 ms intervals, and the more temporally distant bursts in the 1000 ms intervals, are a reflection of the subject's internal maintenance of a visuo-spatial rhythm for the fast and slow tempos, respectively.
evidence: Interpretation of neural activity patterns

claim: Gamma bursts have a similar temporal profile across tempos and elapsed intervals.
source: Alignment of the gamma bursts to their onset time revealed that bursts have a similar temporal profile across tempos and elapsed intervals (Figure 3B).
evidence: Description of analysis result with figure reference

claim: The amplitude of gamma bursts increased in proportion to the time elapsed since the initiation of the internal rhythm (R2 = 0.86, exponential model).
source: Importantly, we found that the amplitude of these bursts increased in proportion to the time elapsed since the initiation of the internal rhythm (Figure 3C; R2 = 0.86, exponential model).
evidence: Quantitative analysis with model fit

claim: LFPs in SMA encode internal rhythms by means of gamma bursts that occur in sync with the beats of a visual metronome presented earlier.
source: The results presented so far indicate that (1) the LFPs in SMA encode internal rhythms by means of gamma bursts that occur in sync with the beats (i.e. location switch) of a visual metronome presented earlier; and that (2) these bursts increase in amplitude, providing a neural correlate for total elapsed time.
evidence: Summary statement of findings

claim: Gamma bursts increase in amplitude, providing a neural correlate for total elapsed time.
source: The results presented so far indicate that (1) the LFPs in SMA encode internal rhythms by means of gamma bursts that occur in sync with the beats (i.e. location switch) of a visual metronome presented earlier; and that (2) these bursts increase in amplitude, providing a neural correlate for total elapsed time.
evidence: Summary statement of findings

claim: Human subjects tend to lag behind fast tempos and get ahead of slow ones.
source: In a previous study, we demonstrated that human subjects tend to lag behind fast tempos and get ahead of slow ones (García-Garibay et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to previous work

claim: Animals might systematically overestimate the 500 ms rhythms and underestimate the 1000 ms rhythms.
source: This predicts that animals might systematically overestimate the 500 ms rhythms, and underestimate the 1000 ms rhythms.
evidence: Prediction based on previous findings

claim: On fast tempo trials (500 ms interval), the dynamics of gamma on error trials was right-shifted with respect to correct trials, displaying slower dynamics.
source: The results showed that, on fast tempo trials (500 ms interval), the dynamics of gamma on error trials was right-shifted with respect to correct trials. That is, error trials displayed slower dynamics compared to correct trials (Figure 4A, upper panel).
evidence: Description of analysis comparing correct and error trials

claim: Error trials on fast tempo (500 ms) oscillated at lower frequencies compared to correct trials.
source: This trend was captured by the power spectrums of error and correct trials, which showed that error trials indeed oscillated at lower frequencies (Figure 4A, inset on upper panel).
evidence: Spectral analysis of error vs correct trials

claim: The dynamics of errors on slow tempo trials (1000 ms) resemble a left-shifted version of correct trials, displaying faster dynamics.
source: Conversely, the dynamics of errors on slow tempo trials (1000 ms) resemble a left-shifted version of the correct trials, that is errors displayed faster dynamics as compared to the correct trials (Figure 4A; bottom panel).
evidence: Description of analysis comparing correct and error trials

claim: Error trials on slow tempo (1000 ms) oscillated at higher frequencies compared to correct trials.
source: This pattern is captured by the power spectrums of correct and error trials, which show that error trials oscillated at higher frequencies compared to correct trials (Figure 4A, inset on the bottom panel).
evidence: Spectral analysis of error vs correct trials

claim: Monkeys were lagging behind fast tempos and getting ahead of slow ones.
source: These results suggest that monkeys were lagging behind fast tempos and getting ahead of slow ones.
evidence: Interpretation of error trial analysis

claim: Correct and error trials can be classified with increasing accuracy as a function of elapsed time.
source: Correct and error trials can be classified with increasing accuracy as a function of elapsed time.
evidence: Description of classifier analysis result

claim: The internal rhythm increasingly getting out of synchrony was demonstrated by the ability of a logistic classifier to differentiate between correct and error trials.
source: The internal rhythm increasingly getting out of synchrony was also demonstrated by the ability of a logistic classifier to differentiate between correct and error trials (Figure 4B; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of classifier analysis

claim: Correct and error trials are increasingly easier to classify as a function of elapsed time, as expected from a rhythm that increasingly falls out of sync with the correct tempo.
source: This analysis shows that correct and error trials are increasingly easier to classify as a function of elapsed time, just as it would be expected from a rhythm that increasingly falls out of sync with the correct tempo.
evidence: Interpretation of classifier results

claim: On average, monkeys tend to lag behind fast rhythms and get ahead of slow ones.
source: On average, monkeys tend lag behind fast rhythms and get ahead of slow ones.
evidence: Summary statement of behavioral pattern

claim: Mean error activity comes from a mixture of lagging and leading tempos.
source: However, we must note that mean error activity comes from a mixture of lagging and leading tempos (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Clarification about composition of error trials with figure reference

claim: Mean error activity does not necessarily reflect the half a cycle de-synchronization that must underlie incorrect responses on single trials.
source: Thus, mean error activity does not necessarily reflect the half a cycle de-synchronization that must underlie incorrect responses on single trials.
evidence: Interpretation of error trial data

claim: SMA participates in the preparation of impending motor actions.
source: Since SMA participates in the preparation of impending motor actions, it is possible that the rhythmic gamma bursts that we observed arise because this premotor area rhythmically prepare reach movements alternatively to the left and right locations of the screen.
evidence: Statement of known function with speculation about mechanism

claim: It is possible that rhythmic gamma bursts arise because SMA rhythmically prepares reach movements alternatively to the left and right locations of the screen.
source: Since SMA participates in the preparation of impending motor actions, it is possible that the rhythmic gamma bursts that we observed arise because this premotor area rhythmically prepare reach movements alternatively to the left and right locations of the screen.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed neural activity

claim: In the delayed-reach control task, subjects were required to reach to the left or right after being cued by a briefly presented visual stimulus.
source: To test this possibility, we recorded the LFPs in a delayed-reach control task (Hwang and Andersen, 2011) in which subjects were required to reach to the left or the right after being cued by a briefly presented visual stimulus (Figure 5A).
evidence: Description of control task with citation

claim: In the delayed-reach task, monkeys waited a pseudo-randomly chosen time (1100 to 3000 ms, exponential distribution) before a go-cue prompted a reach.
source: In this task, monkeys waited a pseudo-randomly chosen time (1100 to 3000 ms, exponential distribution) before a go-cue prompted a reach towards the location specified by the cue (Figure 5B).
evidence: Description of task parameters

claim: As monkeys prepare an impending reach movement, LFPs in SMA generate bursts of gamma band activity that occur more frequently and with increasing amplitude as a function of total elapsed time.
source: The results of this control task show that, as monkeys prepare an impending reach movement, the LFPs in SMA generate bursts of gamma band activity that occur more frequently, and with increasing amplitude, as a function of total elapsed time (Figure 5C, delay period).
evidence: Description of neural activity in control task

claim: The findings from the delayed-reach control task are consistent with the idea that gamma bursts in SMA encode impending motor commands.
source: These findings are consistent with the idea that gamma bursts in SMA encode impending motor commands.
evidence: Interpretation of control task results

claim: The results of the control task are consistent with the idea that SMA circuits reflect internal rhythms by means of rhythmically alternating motor plans to make a reach movement to the left and right locations of the screen.
source: Moreover, the results of this control task are consistent with the idea that the SMA circuits reflect internal rhythms by means of rhythmically alternating motor plans to make a reach movement to the left and right locations of the screen.
evidence: Interpretation connecting control task to main task

claim: The metronome task is designed such that a motor response was never required during the three entrainment intervals.
source: However, our task is designed such that a motor response was never required during the three entrainment intervals.
evidence: Statement of task design

claim: Even during entrainment intervals, which did not involve any motor planning, bursts of gamma oscillations were present in each interval and their amplitude progressively increased after the presentation of each visual stimulus.
source: The results showed that even during entrainment intervals, which did not involve any motor planning, bursts of gamma oscillations were present in each interval, and their amplitude progressively increased after the presentation of each visual stimulus (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Description of neural activity during entrainment

claim: Gamma activity in entrainment intervals peaked after each stimulus presentation, in contrast to maintenance intervals where peaks occurred when the stimulus switched sides.
source: It is important to note that gamma activity in entrainment intervals peaked after each stimulus presentation. This is in contrast to what was observed during maintenance intervals, in which the peaks of gamma occurred when the stimulus switched sides.
evidence: Comparison of neural activity patterns between task epochs

claim: The phase offset between entrainment and maintenance gamma peaks could be related to the process of estimating interval duration.
source: We speculate that this phase offset could be related to the process of estimating interval duration, a process that necessarily happens during entrainment intervals.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed phase difference

claim: A pure sensory response should produce similar gamma dynamics after each stimulus presentation, both across consecutive entrainment intervals and across tempos, which was not the case.
source: However, a pure sensory response should produce similar gamma dynamics after each stimulus presentation, both across consecutive entrainment intervals (1st, 2nd, 3rd), and also similar across tempos (500, 750, 1000 ms), which was clearly not the case in our results (Figure 6A).
evidence: Argument against sensory response interpretation

claim: Gamma bursts during entrainment cannot be explained solely in terms of a sensory response.
source: In particular, two observations suggest that gamma bursts during entrainment cannot be explained solely in terms of a sensory response.
evidence: Statement introducing evidence against sensory interpretation

claim: Gamma bursts increased in amplitude as a function of elapsed time, but the amplitude dropped sharply 500 ms after the onset of the third entrainment interval.
source: First, gamma bursts increased in amplitude as a function of elapsed time, but the amplitude dropped sharply 500 ms after the onset of the third entrainment interval (Figures 6A, 750 and 1000 ms panels).
evidence: Description of specific pattern in neural data

claim: Gamma bursts carry information about the animals' knowledge that the third entrainment interval was the last visible interval.
source: Therefore, gamma bursts carry information about the animals' knowledge that the third entrainment interval was the last visible interval, that is the last interval that could be used for estimating the tempo.
evidence: Interpretation of neural activity pattern

claim: Gamma dynamics likely incorporate aspects of higher cognitive processing.
source: Thus, gamma dynamics likely incorporate aspects of higher cognitive processing.
evidence: Conclusion based on observed patterns

claim: The times of burst onset do not have a fixed temporal profile with respect to stimulus presentation.
source: Second, the times of burst onset do not have a fixed temporal profile with respect to stimulus presentation (Figure 6B).
evidence: Description of variability in neural timing

claim: The temporal profiles of gamma onset times significantly differ both across consecutive intervals and across metronome tempos (p<0.01).
source: The tests demonstrated that the temporal profiles of gamma onset times significantly differ, both across consecutive intervals and across metronome tempos (p<0.01; corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Statistical test of burst timing distributions

claim: Gamma responses to stimulus onset are similar only during the first 500 ms of the first entrainment interval, which is the only epoch in which monkeys have no information about the metronome tempo.
source: In fact, gamma responses to stimulus onset are similar only during the first 500 ms of the first entrainment interval, which is the only epoch in which monkeys have no information about the metronome tempo (Figure 6C).
evidence: Description of when neural responses are similar across conditions

claim: Gamma bursts reflect cognitive processes related to estimating the rhythm of the visual metronome.
source: These results indicate that gamma bursts reflect cognitive processes related to estimating the rhythm of the visual metronome.
evidence: Interpretation of neural activity patterns

claim: Burst amplitude increased linearly in proportion to total elapsed time during entrainment intervals (R2 = 0.94).
source: We found that burst amplitude increased linearly in proportion to total elapsed time (R2 = 0.94).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of burst amplitude

claim: In addition to periodically generating bursts in each entrainment interval, the SMA circuit reflected the total elapsed time since the beginning of the entrainment epoch.
source: In this manner, in addition to periodically generating bursts in each entrainment interval, the SMA circuit reflected the total elapsed time since the beginning of the entrainment epoch.
evidence: Summary of dual encoding in neural activity

claim: 113 neurons were recorded (78 from monkey 1 and 35 from monkey 2).
source: Simultaneously with LFPs, we recorded the extracellular spike potentials of 113 neurons (78 monkey 1; 35 monkey 2).
evidence: Statement of data collection

claim: The temporal profile of mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP.
source: The temporal profile of the mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP in the sense that firing rates (1) display oscillatory amplitude modulations, both during entrainment and maintenance intervals (Figure 7A,B); (2) firing rates increase as a function of total elapsed time; and (3) the activity of neurons in the delayed-reach task increase during the period preceding reach movements to a target signaled by a brief visual cue (Figure 7C).
evidence: Description of similarity between spiking and LFP patterns

claim: Firing rates display oscillatory amplitude modulations during both entrainment and maintenance intervals.
source: The temporal profile of the mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP in the sense that firing rates (1) display oscillatory amplitude modulations, both during entrainment and maintenance intervals (Figure 7A,B); (2) firing rates increase as a function of total elapsed time; and (3) the activity of neurons in the delayed-reach task increase during the period preceding reach movements to a target signaled by a brief visual cue (Figure 7C).
evidence: Description of firing rate patterns

claim: Firing rates increase as a function of total elapsed time.
source: The temporal profile of the mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP in the sense that firing rates (1) display oscillatory amplitude modulations, both during entrainment and maintenance intervals (Figure 7A,B); (2) firing rates increase as a function of total elapsed time; and (3) the activity of neurons in the delayed-reach task increase during the period preceding reach movements to a target signaled by a brief visual cue (Figure 7C).
evidence: Description of firing rate patterns

claim: The activity of neurons in the delayed-reach task increases during the period preceding reach movements to a target signaled by a brief visual cue.
source: The temporal profile of the mean firing rates largely resembled the modulations of gamma-band activity in the LFP in the sense that firing rates (1) display oscillatory amplitude modulations, both during entrainment and maintenance intervals (Figure 7A,B); (2) firing rates increase as a function of total elapsed time; and (3) the activity of neurons in the delayed-reach task increase during the period preceding reach movements to a target signaled by a brief visual cue (Figure 7C).
evidence: Description of neural activity in control task

claim: SMA neurons had a preferred spatial location, being more active when the stimulus was presented or estimated to be on one side of the screen.
source: We found that SMA neurons had a preferred spatial location, that is they were more active when the stimulus was presented (entrainment intervals), or was estimated to be (maintenance intervals), on one side of the screen.
evidence: Description of spatial selectivity in neural responses

claim: Of the 113 recorded neurons, 74 preferred the right side of the screen and 39 preferred the left side.
source: Of the 113 recorded neurons, 74 preferred the right side of the screen, and 39 preferred the left side (Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantification of spatial preferences

claim: The cross-correlation analysis between firing rates provided independent corroboration that errors are mostly due to the internal metronome lagging behind fast rhythms and getting ahead of slow ones.
source: The cross-correlation analysis between firing rates provided an independent corroboration of the hypothesis that that errors are mostly due to the internal metronome lagging behind fast rhythms, and getting ahead of slow ones (Figure 7E).
evidence: Description of cross-correlation analysis results

claim: The cross-correlogram for the 500 and 750 ms intervals peak at negative lags, demonstrating that incorrect trials lag behind the correct tempo.
source: The cross-correlogram for the 500 and 750 ms intervals peak at negative lags, demonstrating that incorrect trials lag behind the correct tempo.
evidence: Description of cross-correlation results

claim: For the slow tempo (1000 ms), the opposite pattern was observed, with errors getting ahead of the correct tempo.
source: The opposite pattern was observed for the slow tempo (1000 ms tempo).
evidence: Description of cross-correlation results for slow tempo

claim: The LFP activity simultaneously recorded with each spike has a power peak at 30 Hz, especially salient during maintenance intervals.
source: We found that the LFP activity simultaneously recorded with each spike has a power peak at 30 Hz, and this peak is especially salient during maintenance intervals (Figure 8A, bottom panel; factorial ANOVA: interaction band/condition F = 12.11 p<0.05, Bonferroni tests of Gamma power in maintenance and entrainment vs baseline: p<0.05).
evidence: Spike-triggered average analysis with statistical tests

claim: The association between spikes and the 25-40 Hz frequency band is stronger at the times of stimulus transitions.
source: Moreover, the association between spikes and the 25–40 Hz frequency band is stronger at the times of stimulus transitions, that is. around the times at which the stimulus switches from one side of the screen to the other (Figure 8C; window length around switch: half an interval, t-test p<0.005).
evidence: Statistical comparison of spike-LFP association at different task phases

claim: Jittering spike times by ±15 ms resulted in loss of the observed peak at the gamma band.
source: To demonstrate that gamma is closely associated with the timing of spikes we performed a control analysis in which we jittered the spike times by ±15 ms with the resulting loss of the observed peak at the gamma band (random uniform distribution; grey traces Figure 8c; t test between jittered data in switch and non-switch conditions p=0.21).
evidence: Control analysis demonstrating temporal specificity

claim: The performance of the metronome task is accompanied by a tighter temporal relationship between gamma bursts and the firing of single neurons, more prominent at times of stimulus switching during maintenance intervals.
source: These analyses demonstrate that the performance of the metronome task is accompanied by a tighter temporal relationship between the gamma bursts and the firing of single neurons, and this association is more prominent at the times of stimulus switching during the maintenance intervals.
evidence: Summary of spike-LFP relationship analysis

claim: LFP oscillations near gamma frequencies could help single neurons synchronize their firing and have a larger and more temporally precise influence on downstream target structures.
source: These results are consistent with previous investigations proposing that LFP oscillations near the gamma frequencies could help single neurons synchronize their firing, and thus have a larger and more temporally precise influence on downstream target structures (Siegle et al., 2014; Veit et al., 2017; Fries, 2015).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to supporting literature

claim: The LFP signals recorded reflect local interaction and were not the result of signals being volume-conducted from other brain regions.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the LFP signals we recorded reflect local interaction and were not the result of signals being volume-conducted from other brain regions.
evidence: Statement about signal source

claim: Coherence between LFPs of simultaneously recorded electrodes decayed as a function of electrode distance (R2 = 0.72).
source: We measured the coherence between LFPs of simultaneously recorded electrodes and plotted this measure as a function of the distance between them. The results show that coherence decayed as a function of electrode distance (Figure 8D, R2 = 0.72), as expected by an LFP signal that is generated in the neuronal circuits within the vicinity of the recording electrode.
evidence: Analysis of spatial coherence with interpretation

claim: Monkeys can maintain rhythms in the absence of sensory stimuli and in the absence of overt motor commands.
source: Our results show that (1) monkeys can maintain rhythms in the absence of sensory stimuli and in the absence of overt motor commands.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: Internal rhythms are encoded by bursts of low gamma-band LFP oscillations in SMA whose timing and amplitude indicate rhythm intervals and total elapsed time, respectively.
source: Our results show that (1) monkeys can maintain rhythms in the absence of sensory stimuli and in the absence of overt motor commands. (2) Those internal rhythms are encoded by bursts of low gamma-band LFP oscillations in SMA whose timing and amplitude indicate rhythm intervals and total elapsed time, respectively.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding

claim: The spikes of single neurons are associated with the low gamma band frequency of the LFP.
source: (3) The spikes of single neurons are associated with the low gamma band frequency of the LFP, which is consistent with the idea that gamma oscillations might help to synchronize populations of neurons whose temporally coincident firing would have a larger impact on its postsynaptic targets (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Cardin et al., 2009; Fries, 2015; Siegle et al., 2014; Veit et al., 2017; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary statement with citations to supporting literature

claim: Gamma oscillations might help to synchronize populations of neurons whose temporally coincident firing would have a larger impact on postsynaptic targets.
source: (3) The spikes of single neurons are associated with the low gamma band frequency of the LFP, which is consistent with the idea that gamma oscillations might help to synchronize populations of neurons whose temporally coincident firing would have a larger impact on its postsynaptic targets (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015; Cardin et al., 2009; Fries, 2015; Siegle et al., 2014; Veit et al., 2017; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation with extensive citations

claim: In the metronome task, there is a rhythmic modulation in the likelihood of motor response initiation.
source: In our metronome task, the go-cue can arrive at the middle of any of the four maintenance intervals. So, there is a rhythmic modulation in the likelihood of motor response initiation.
evidence: Statement about task structure

claim: The rhythmic modulation in response likelihood could be related to the periodic modulation of gamma bursts and firing rates of SMA neurons.
source: This could be related the periodic modulation of the gamma bursts and the firing rates of SMA neurons.
evidence: Speculative connection between task structure and neural activity

claim: The rhythmicity in gamma bursts and firing rates is also observed in entrainment intervals, where no movement is ever required.
source: However, we must emphasize that the rhythmicity in the gamma bursts and firing rates is also observed in entrainment intervals, where no movement is ever required.
evidence: Observation that argues against pure motor preparation interpretation

claim: The probability of the go-cue appearing increases as a function of total elapsed time (hazard rate).
source: In addition to rhythmic modulations, the probability of the go-cue appearing, given that it has not appeared yet, increases as a function of total elapsed time (hazard rate).
evidence: Description of task structure

claim: The increase in gamma amplitude and firing rates as total time elapses could be related to the increasing likelihood of a motor response.
source: Thus, the increase in gamma amplitude and in the firing rates that is observed as total time elapses, could be related to the increasing likelihood of a motor response.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed pattern

claim: In the delayed-reach task, an exponential distribution of delay times was used, resulting in a flat hazard rate.
source: We must note, however, that in the delayed-reach task we used an exponential distribution of delay times, resulting in a flat hazard rate.
evidence: Description of control task design

claim: Even with a flat hazard rate in the delayed-reach task, increases in gamma amplitude and firing rates related to total elapsed time were observed.
source: Even with a flat hazard rate, we observed increases in gamma amplitude, and in the firing rates, that are related to total elapsed time.
evidence: Observation from control task

claim: SMA participates in the metronome task by generating a motor plan that dynamically matches the spatio-temporal tempo defined by the rhythmic visual stimulus.
source: Overall, we favor the interpretation that SMA participates in the metronome task by generating a motor plan that dynamically matches the spatio-temporal tempo defined by the rhythmic visual stimulus.
evidence: Authors' preferred interpretation of findings

claim: SMA plays a central role in learning, imaging, planning and executing complex motor actions.
source: SMA plays a central role in learning, imaging, planning and executing complex motor actions (Nachev et al., 2008; Romo and Schultz, 1992; Kurata and Wise, 1988; Shima and Tanji, 2000; Murakami et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement of known function with citations

claim: SMA is densely and reciprocally connected to M1 and to the parietal and frontal lobes, and has direct projections to motor nuclei in the brain stem.
source: It is densely and reciprocally connected to M1 and to the parietal and frontal lobes, and has direct projections to motor nuclei in the brain stem (Jürgens, 1984).
evidence: Statement of anatomical connectivity with citation

claim: SMA activity has been found to correlate not only with motor actions but also with cognitive, emotional, and perceptual functions.
source: Thanks to this diverse input and output relationships its activity been found to correlate not only with motor actions but also with cognitive, emotional, and perceptual functions (Narayana et al., 2012; Vergara et al., 2016; de Lafuente and Romo, 2005).
evidence: Statement of functional diversity with citations

claim: SMA is active before actual movement begins, participating in action selection and determining the time at which actions are performed.
source: SMA is active before the actual movement begins, participating in action selection, and importantly, determining the time at which actions are performed (Merchant and Averbeck, 2017; Mita et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2010; Ohara et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 2016; Shima and Tanji, 2000).
evidence: Statement of temporal dynamics with citations

claim: Preparatory activity can be observed even when monkeys are required to rapidly produce a movement in response to a sensory cue.
source: Preparatory activity can be observed even when monkeys are required to rapidly produce a movement in response to a sensory cue (Lara et al., 2018), and it has been proposed that this preparatory activity constitutes the initial step of the temporal evolution of a dynamical system for the control of movement (Churchland et al., 2010; Remington et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about preparatory activity with citations

claim: Preparatory activity constitutes the initial step of the temporal evolution of a dynamical system for the control of movement.
source: Preparatory activity can be observed even when monkeys are required to rapidly produce a movement in response to a sensory cue (Lara et al., 2018), and it has been proposed that this preparatory activity constitutes the initial step of the temporal evolution of a dynamical system for the control of movement (Churchland et al., 2010; Remington et al., 2018).
evidence: Theoretical framework with citations

claim: LFP and single neuron activity in SMA starts during the entrainment epoch of the metronome task, seconds before an actual movement will be required.
source: Consistent with this view, our results show that LFP and single neuron activity in SMA starts during the entrainment epoch of the metronome task, seconds before an actual movement will be required.
evidence: Description of temporal dynamics in current data

claim: The internal metronome is encoded as a dynamic motor plan that is initiated by the presentation of entrainment intervals.
source: Thus, the internal metronome is encoded as a dynamic motor plan that is initiated by the presentation of entrainment intervals.
evidence: Interpretation of findings

claim: The tempo of the internal metronome is encoded by the timing, not the amplitude of the gamma bursts.
source: However, we must note that the tempo of the internal metronome is encoded by the timing, not the amplitude of the gamma bursts.
evidence: Clarification of encoding mechanism

claim: Error trials are not explained by random behavioral responses but by the internal metronome lagging or getting ahead of the true tempo.
source: Instead, the behavioral responses on the six-choice version of the task demonstrate that error trials are due to the internal metronome lagging or getting ahead of the true tempo.
evidence: Interpretation of behavioral data from six-choice task

claim: Even on error trials, gamma activity and firing patterns show rhythmic dynamics and a mean amplitude that increases with total elapsed time.
source: Even on error trials, gamma activity, and the firing pattern of neurons, show rhythmic dynamics and a mean amplitude that increases with total elapsed time.
evidence: Description of neural activity on error trials

claim: There are three independent lines of evidence supporting that error trials arise from the internal metronome falling out of sync with the intended tempo.
source: Thus, there are three independent lines of evidence supporting the notion that error trials arise from the internal metronome falling out of sync with the intended tempo.
evidence: Summary statement introducing evidence

claim: The periodograms of gamma activity indicate that errors on fast trials (500 ms) oscillate at slower frequencies compared to correct trials.
source: First, the periodograms of gamma activity indicate that errors on fast trials (500 ms interval) oscillate at slower frequencies as compared to correct trials.
evidence: Summary of spectral analysis result

claim: Errors on slow tempos (1000 ms) oscillate faster than correct responses.
source: Conversely, errors on slow tempos (1000 ms) oscillate faster than correct responses.
evidence: Summary of spectral analysis result

claim: The cross-correlograms of firing rates in correct and incorrect trials showed the same patterns as the gamma periodograms.
source: Second, these same patterns were demonstrated by the cross-correlograms of the firing rates in correct and incorrect trials (Figure 7E).
evidence: Summary of cross-correlation analysis

claim: Behavioral results on the six-choice version showed that errors are not uniformly distributed across choices but distribute around the correct stimulus position with increasing variability for longer elapsed times.
source: Finally, the behavioral results on the six-choice version of the metronome task showed that errors are not uniformly distributed across choices (as would be expected from lapses of attention), but distribute around the correct stimulus position, with increasing variability for longer elapsed times, as would be expected from the scalar property of timing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of behavioral error distribution

claim: The error distributions show that errors tend to be behind the true stimulus position on fast trials and ahead on slow trials.
source: Moreover, the distributions show that errors tend to be behind the true stimulus position on fast trials, and ahead on slow trials.
evidence: Description of error pattern

claim: It has been debated whether subjects performing a rhythmic task measure individual intervals separately or rely on an estimate of total elapsed time.
source: It has been debated whether subjects performing a rhythmic task measure individual intervals separately, or instead rely on an estimate of total elapsed time (Laje et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement of existing debate with citation

claim: Rhythms of different tempos are supported by the presence of rhythmic neuronal activity outlining each individual interval.
source: Our results now reveal that rhythms of different tempos are supported by the presence of rhythmic neuronal activity outlining each individual interval.
evidence: Summary of finding addressing debate

claim: In addition to rhythmic activity, the increases in gamma burst amplitude and mean firing rates provide information about total elapsed time.
source: In addition to this, the increases in gamma burst amplitude, and mean firing rates, provide information about total elapsed time.
evidence: Summary of dual encoding finding

claim: Gamma synchronization might be useful to the formation of local ensembles of neurons that increase the temporal coordination of presynaptic spikes on postsynaptic targets.
source: Gamma synchronization might be useful to the formation of local ensembles of neurons that increase the temporal coordination of presynaptic spikes on postsynaptic targets, allowing brief windows of effective communication (Wong et al., 2016; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation with citations

claim: Gamma oscillations increase before the execution of a motor action and then shut down at the time of movement onset.
source: Previous results show that gamma oscillations increase before the execution of a motor action, and then shut down at the time of movement onset (Yokoyama et al., 2016) a result replicated by our data.
evidence: Statement of previous finding with citation and confirmation in current data

claim: Previous work by Merchant and colleagues found that LFP gamma band activity in the basal ganglia was associated with the presentation of sensory stimuli defining intervals within a hand tapping task.
source: Previous work by Merchant and colleagues found that LFP gamma band activity in the basal ganglia was associated with the presentation of sensory stimuli defining the intervals within a hand tapping task (Bartolo et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of previous work with citation

claim: Merchant and colleagues found that bursts of gamma were selective for intervals of different durations, with different cell populations selective for different time intervals.
source: They found that bursts of gamma were selective for intervals of different durations, and thus different cell populations were selective for different time intervals.
evidence: Summary of previous findings

claim: No duration selectivity was found in the SMA cortex; instead, gamma bursts encoded intervals of different durations.
source: We found no such duration selectivity in the SMA cortex, instead observing that gamma bursts encoded intervals of different durations.
evidence: Contrast between current findings and previous work

claim: Signals associated with timing tasks can be found across multiple brain areas, including parietal, motor, and premotor cortices, as well as dopaminergic midbrain neurons in the primate.
source: Signals associated with timing tasks can be found across multiple brain areas, including parietal, motor, and premotor cortices, as well as dopaminergic midbrain neuron in the primate (Ghose and Maunsell, 2002; Genovesio et al., 2006; Lebedev and Wise, 2000; Mita et al., 2009; Harrington et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement of distributed timing signals with citations

claim: Jazayeri and Shadlen showed that activity of single neurons in the lateral intraparietal area encodes the time elapsed from a previous sensory stimulus and the time remaining to initiate a saccadic eye movement.
source: For example, Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015 have shown that activity of single neurons in the lateral intraparietal area encodes the time elapsed from a previous sensory stimuli, as well as the time remaining to initiate a saccadic eye movement (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2015).
evidence: Summary of previous work with citation

claim: Jazayeri and Shadlen showed that timing signals calibrate themselves according to the underlying probability to make an eye movement within a given temporal window.
source: Importantly, they showed that these signals calibrate themselves according to the underlying probability to make an eye movement within a given temporal window.
evidence: Summary of previous finding

claim: Jazayeri and colleagues demonstrated that encoding intervals of different lengths is achieved by speeding up or slowing down the temporal dynamics of populations of neurons.
source: A recent important result by Jazayeri and colleagues demonstrated that encoding intervals of different lengths is achieved by means of speeding up or slowing down the temporal dynamics of populations of neurons that, individually, display widely different firing patterns (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of recent work with citation

claim: The current results extend the finding of temporal scaling to the dynamics of LFP oscillations.
source: Our results extend this finding to the dynamics of the LFP oscillations by demonstrating that they also show temporal scaling (Figures 3A and 6C).
evidence: Statement connecting current findings to previous work

claim: Time-estimation and time-production signals are present as dynamic motor plans distributed across motor structures that participate in executing timely motor actions.
source: A coherent picture is thus emerging, indicating that time-estimation and time-production signals are present as dynamic motor plans that are distributed across the motor structures that participate in executing timely motor actions.
evidence: Synthesis of current and previous findings

claim: Neural recordings were performed with seven independent movable microelectrodes (2-3 MΩ).
source: Neural recordings were performed with seven independent movable microelectrodes (2–3 MΩ, Thomas Recordings, Giessen, Germany).
evidence: Description of recording methods

claim: Electrodes were advanced into the supplementary motor area until single unit activity was obtained in at least one electrode.
source: Electrodes were advanced in the coronal plane into the supplementary motor area until single unit activity was obtained in at least one of the electrodes.
evidence: Description of recording procedure

claim: Spikes were isolated online and sampled at 30 KHz.
source: At each recording site, spikes were isolated online (Cerebus acquisition system, Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT) and sampled at 30 KHz.
evidence: Description of data acquisition

claim: Local field potentials were obtained by filtering the electrode signal at 0.5 to 500 Hz at a 2 KHz rate.
source: The local field potentials (LFPs) were obtained by filtering the electrode signal at 0.5 to 500 Hz, at a 2 KHz rate.
evidence: Description of LFP processing

claim: Offline, the LFP signal was down sampled to 1 KHz and band-pass filtered to the 2-50 Hz band.
source: Offline, the signal was down sampled to 1 KHz, and band-pass filtered to the 2–50 Hz band.
evidence: Description of offline processing

claim: Spectral estimation was performed using multitaper methods with a 200 ms window sliding at 5 ms steps.
source: Spectral estimation was performed using multitaper methods (Pesaran et al., 2002; Mitra and Pesaran, 1999; Cohen, 2014). A 200 ms windows sliding at 5 ms steps was used for the time-frequency maps (one taper was used, 5 Hz bandwidth).
evidence: Description of spectral analysis methods with citations

claim: Spectrogram power was normalized by dividing each frequency and time bin by the average power in a 500 ms baseline window before trial initiation.
source: Spectrogram power was normalized by dividing each frequency and time bin by the average power in a 500 ms baseline window before trial initiation.
evidence: Description of normalization procedure

claim: Gamma bursts were defined as periods when gamma amplitude exceeded the 90th percentile of overall activity for at least 100 ms.
source: Gamma bursts were defined as the period of time in which gamma amplitude exceeded the 90th percentile of overall activity for at least 100 ms (i.e. for at least four cycles of the gamma oscillations).
evidence: Definition of analysis criterion

claim: A logistic function was used to classify correct and error trials based on gamma amplitude in time bins.
source: A logistic function was used to identify correct and error trials
evidence: Description of classification method

claim: The classifier accuracy was measured on 100 trials (50 correct and 50 error trials) not used in fitting the logistic function.
source: The classifier accuracy was measured on 100 trials (50 correct and 50 error trials; randomly selected) not used in fitting the logistic function.
evidence: Description of cross-validation procedure

claim: Each neuron's spatial preference was estimated by computing the cross-correlation between stimulus position and mean firing rate.
source: To estimate each neuron's spatial preference, we computed the cross-correlation between the stimulus position (left and right) and the mean firing rate.
evidence: Description of analysis method

claim: To estimate synchronization between spikes and LFP, 200 ms windows centered on each spike were analyzed.
source: To estimate the synchronization between the spikes and the simultaneously recorded LFP, 200 ms windows centered on each spike were analyzed (Fries et al., 2001; Denker et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of spike-triggered average method with citations

claim: A factorial ANOVA demonstrated that the average power of the STA over the gamma band was significantly larger during entrainment and maintenance compared to baseline (p<0.01).
source: This analysis demonstrated that the average power of the STA over the gamma band was significantly larger during entrainment and maintenance, as compared to the baseline period (p<0.01; Figure 8B).
evidence: Statistical test result

claim: Coherence between electrode pairs was defined as the length of the average vector of all phase difference angles.
source: The coherence was defined as the length of the average vector of all difference angles, a procedure that results in magnitudes between 1 (all difference angles are aligned to the same direction) and zero (random distribution) (Cohen, 2014).
evidence: Definition of coherence measure with citation
